sounds.intro: This is the restored pronunciation of educated Romans in Cicero's day, as set out by W. Sidney Allen in Vox Latina (2nd ed. 1978). The evidence is good: Roman grammarians describe the sounds, Greeks wrote Cicerō as Kikerōn and Caesar as Kaisar, misspellings on Pompeii's walls show how people really talked, and the Romance languages keep traces of the old vowels. The consonants and vowel length are secure; a few details, such as final m, are educated guesses.

rows.like: short like 'cup' in southern British English, long like 'father'
short like 'pet', long like 'hey' held without the glide
short like British 'pot', long like French 'beau'

rows.note: It later flattened to e, as in Church Latin.

rows.like: two vowels in one syllable: 'day', e + oo, oo + ee
always hard, as in 'cat', even before e and i

rows.note: V and U were one letter: Romans carved VENI VIDI VICI.
Between vowels it was doubled: maior sounded like mai-yor.

rows.like: as in 'hat', but weak; country speech dropped it

rows.like: b becomes 'p' before s and t
rows.note: Quintilian (1.7.7) says obtinuit is spelled with b by rule, but the ear hears p.

rows.like: p, t and k with a puff of breath, as in 'pot', 'top', 'kit'; never 'f' or English 'th'
rows.note: Used only in Greek words. Ordinary speakers often said plain p, t, c.
Only in Greek words; many Romans probably said u or i.

tips.p: A long vowel lasts about twice as long as a short one, and length can change the word: mālum 'apple', malum 'evil'; līber 'free', liber 'book'; vēnit 'he came', venit 'he comes'.
Doubled letters are held, as in Italian: bel-lum, not belum. anus 'old woman' and annus 'year' differ only in the n.

Two-syllable words stress the first syllable: PA-ter. Longer words stress the second-to-last syllable if it is heavy, that is if it has a long vowel, a diphthong, or a vowel followed by two consonants (x counts as two): a-MĪ-cus, pu-EL-la. Otherwise the stress falls one syllable earlier: FĒ-mi-na, MĪ-li-tēs. It never goes further back than that.
A final -m was barely sounded. It probably just made the vowel nasal, so puellam came out close to French-style puellã, and in poetry it disappeared before a following vowel.

The Catholic Church and most choirs use an Italian-style pronunciation: c before e, i, ae and oe is 'ch' (Cicerō is 'Chichero'), g before e and i is 'j', v is English 'v', ae and oe are both 'e', ti before a vowel is 'tsi', sc before e and i is 'sh', gn is 'ny', and h is silent (mihi is often 'miki'). Vowel length is mostly ignored. It is a fine living tradition, just a later one than Cicero's.

The consonants and the long and short vowels are secure. Still debated: the exact quality of the short vowels, final m, the Greek sounds, and whether the stressed syllable was louder or higher in pitch.

grammar.title: The cases
grammar.note: Endings show each word's job, so word order is free. The lessons drill the nominative, accusative and ablative; the genitive and dative turn up in the stories.

grammar.title: First declension: puella 'girl'
grammar.note: Most nouns in -a, nearly all feminine. A few that name men's jobs, like poēta 'poet', are masculine.
head: Singular
Plural

grammar.title: Second declension: amīcus 'friend'
grammar.note: Mostly masculine. Calling someone uses -e: Brūte! puer and liber keep -er in the nominative: puer, puerum; liber, librum.
head: Singular
Plural

grammar.title: Second declension neuter: vīnum 'wine'
grammar.note: Neuters never change between subject and object, and their plural always ends in -a.
head: Singular
Plural

grammar.title: Third declension: rēx 'king'
grammar.note: The nominative often hides the stem, so learn another form with the word: urbs, urbem; mīles, mīlitem; pāx, pācem. Some, like urbs, hostis and mare, have -ium in the genitive plural.
head: Singular
Plural

grammar.title: Present tense
grammar.note: The ending is the pronoun. These are the four conjugations, plus sum. edit, bibit and vincit go like regit.
head: amō 'love'
videō 'see'
regō 'rule'
veniō 'come'
sum 'be'

grammar.title: Personal pronouns
grammar.note: Used only for emphasis, since the verb ending already says who. cum 'with' goes on the end: mēcum 'with me', tēcum 'with you'.
head: I
you
we
you (plural)

grammar.title: Commands
grammar.note: The singular is the bare stem. dīcere, dūcere and facere drop the e: dīc, dūc, fac. To say 'don't', use nōlī with the infinitive: nōlī timēre 'don't be afraid'.
head: Verb
To one person
To several

grammar.title: Perfect tense
grammar.note: Every verb puts the same endings on its own perfect stem. Watch the vowel: venit 'he comes', vēnit 'he came'.
head: amāvī 'I loved'
vīdī 'I saw'
vēnī 'I came'
fuī 'I was'

grammar.title: Principal parts
grammar.note: Dictionaries list a verb by these forms, plus a fourth, the participle. The perfect is often unpredictable, so learn them together.
head: Present
Infinitive
Perfect

grammar.title: Plurals at a glance
grammar.note: A plural subject takes a plural verb: est becomes sunt, amat becomes amant, vēnit becomes vēnērunt.
head: Singular
Plural subject
Plural object

grammar.title: Third declension neuter: corpus 'body'
grammar.note: Like all neuters, the same as subject and object, with a plural in -a. nōmen, tempus and flūmen work the same way: nōmina, tempora, flūmina.
head: Singular
Plural

grammar.title: Adjectives: bonus, bona, bonum 'good'
grammar.note: Masculine goes like amīcus, feminine like puella, neuter like vīnum. magnus, parvus, longus, malus and sānus all work this way.
head: Masculine

grammar.title: Adjectives: fortis, forte 'brave'
grammar.note: Third-declension adjectives. Note the -ī in the ablative and -ium in the genitive plural. The accusative plural can also be fortīs.
head: Masculine and feminine
Neuter

grammar.title: Comparison
grammar.note: Comparatives decline in the third declension, with a neuter in -ius: longius, melius, maius. Superlatives go like bonus. 'Than' is quam.
head: Adjective

grammar.title: Relative pronoun: quī, quae, quod
grammar.note: Gender and number come from the noun it refers to, case from its job in its own clause: deus quem vidēs 'the god whom you see'.

grammar.note: 'Was doing' or 'used to do': the background of a story. The -ba- never changes.

grammar.title: Future tense
grammar.note: amō and videō verbs use -b-; regō and veniō verbs use -a- then -e-. Careful: reget 'he will rule', regit 'he rules'.

grammar.title: possum 'can' and volō 'want'
grammar.note: Both take an infinitive: Rōmam vidēre volō 'I want to see Rome'. possum is pot- + sum.
